## Introduction

As objects move in the world, or as the camera moves, the projection of
the dynamic scene into the two-dimensional (2D) camera plane produces a
sequence of temporally varying pixel brightness. Before diving into how
to estimate motion from pixels, it is useful to understand the image
formation process. Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects
into the camera will allow us to understand what the difference is
between a moving camera or a moving object and what types of constraints
one might be able to use to estimate motion.

## 3D Motion and Its 2D Projection {#d-motion-and-its-2d-projection}

A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$,
in camera coordinates (@fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the
point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of
$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The
projection of this point into the image plane location is
$\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D
instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
where all the derivatives are done with respect to time, $t$.

![A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.](figures/optical_flow/basic_motion_point.png){width="50%" #fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point}

Using the equations of perspective projection $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$
(assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate
system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity
in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\
\dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} 
\end{aligned}$$ The second expression is obtained by using $x=f \, X/Z$
and $y=f \, Y/Z$, which removes the dependency on the world coordinates
$X$ and $Y$. Note that $f$ is the focal length. In many derivations, the
notation is simplified by setting the focal length $f=1$. Here we will
keep it to make explicit which factors depend on the camera parameters
and which ones do not. We can write the last two equations in matrix
form as:

elements: Origin O (small black sphere representing projection center)
Image plane (semi-transparent gray rectangle at Z = f, with a dark wireframe border)
3D point P (black sphere)
Projected 2D point p (black sphere on the image plane)
Instantaneous 3D velocity vector dot_P (bold red arrow starting at P)
Instantaneous 2D velocity vector dot_p (bold red arrow starting at p on the image plane)
Primary ray (solid green line connecting O, p, and P)
Future/tangent ray (dashed green line connecting O through the tip of dot_p to the tip of dot_P)
Text labels: 'O', 'P', 'p', 'Ṗ', 'ṗ' positioned next to their respective points and vectors

interactions.label: Point Depth (Z)
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates that the magnitude of 2D optical flow is inversely proportional to depth (1/Z scaling) for a constant 3D velocity.

interactions.label: Motion Direction
interactions.teaches: Toggles between lateral motion (producing simple translation on the image plane) and forward motion (producing radial contraction/expansion flow).

demo_steps.title: 3D to 2D Velocity Projection
demo_steps.narration: Observe how the 3D velocity vector Ṗ (red arrow at P) projects onto the image plane as the 2D velocity vector ṗ (red arrow at p). The geometry is locked: the dashed green line connects the tips of both velocity vectors back to the projection center O.

demo_steps.title: Depth Scaling (The 1/Z Effect)
demo_steps.narration: Increase the depth of point P to Z=10. Even though the 3D velocity vector Ṗ maintains the exact same speed, the projected 2D flow vector ṗ shrinks dramatically. This visualizes why distant objects appear to move slower in your field of view.

demo_steps.title: Forward Motion & Radial Flow
demo_steps.narration: Switch the motion direction to 'Toward Camera' (pure Z-velocity). The flow is now dominated by the Z-dot term in the equation, pointing radially outward from the optical center. The 2D speed is now proportional to the point's displacement from the center of the image.

sequence of temporally varying pixel brightness. Before diving into how
to estimate motion from pixels, it is useful to understand the image
formation process. Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects
into the camera will allow us to understand what the difference is
between a moving camera or a moving object and what types of constraints
one might be able to use to estimate motion.

## 3D Motion and Its 2D Projection {#d-motion-and-its-2d-projection}

A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$,
in camera coordinates (@fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the
point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of
$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The
projection of this point into the image plane location is
$\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D
instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
where all the derivatives are done with respect to time, $t$.

![A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.](figures/optical_flow/basic_motion_point.png){width="50%" #fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point}

Using the equations of perspective projection $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$
(assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate
system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity
in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\
\dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} 
\end{aligned}$$ The second expression is obtained by using $x=f \, X/Z$
and $y=f \, Y/Z$, which removes the dependency on the world coordinates
$X$ and $Y$. Note that $f$ is the focal length. In many derivations, the
notation is simplified by setting the focal length $f=1$. Here we will
keep it to make explicit which factors depend on the camera parameters
and which ones do not. We can write the last two equations in matrix
form as:

Image plane (semi-transparent gray rectangle at Z = f, with a dark wireframe border)
3D point P (black sphere)
Projected 2D point p (black sphere on the image plane)
Instantaneous 3D velocity vector dot_P (bold red arrow starting at P)
Instantaneous 2D velocity vector dot_p (bold red arrow starting at p on the image plane)
Primary ray (solid green line connecting O, p, and P)
Future/tangent ray (dashed green line connecting O through the tip of dot_p to the tip of dot_P)
Text labels: 'O', 'P', 'p', 'Ṗ', 'ṗ' positioned next to their respective points and vectors

interactions.label: Point Depth (Z)
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates that the magnitude of 2D optical flow is inversely proportional to depth (1/Z scaling) for a constant 3D velocity.

interactions.label: Motion Direction
interactions.teaches: Toggles between lateral motion (producing simple translation on the image plane) and forward motion (producing radial contraction/expansion flow).

demo_steps.title: 3D to 2D Velocity Projection
demo_steps.narration: Observe how the 3D velocity vector Ṗ (red arrow at P) projects onto the image plane as the 2D velocity vector ṗ (red arrow at p). The geometry is locked: the dashed green line connects the tips of both velocity vectors back to the projection center O.

demo_steps.title: Depth Scaling (The 1/Z Effect)
demo_steps.narration: Increase the depth of point P to Z=10. Even though the 3D velocity vector Ṗ maintains the exact same speed, the projected 2D flow vector ṗ shrinks dramatically. This visualizes why distant objects appear to move slower in your field of view.

demo_steps.title: Forward Motion & Radial Flow
demo_steps.narration: Switch the motion direction to 'Toward Camera' (pure Z-velocity). The flow is now dominated by the Z-dot term in the equation, pointing radially outward from the optical center. The 2D speed is now proportional to the point's displacement from the center of the image.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis:
The developer built three distinct forms of interactivity:
1. A Depth Slider (Z) which dynamically moves the 3D point P, recalculates its projection p, and scales the projected velocity vector to show the 1/Z optical flow effect.
2. A Motion Direction dropdown with 'Lateral' and 'Toward Camera' options, which changes the 3D velocity vector direction and demonstrates translation vs radial expansion.
3. Interactive 3D mesh clicking (on point P, point p, velocity arrows, etc.) using `registerInteractive` that triggers explanatory popups and acts as an animated, step-by-step guided demo of the three key scenarios mapped in the interaction plan.
All elements are functional and pedagogically aligned with the text context.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: The figure beautifully and accurately illustrates all core concepts: (1) perspective projection of a 3D point P to 2D image point p via a projection ray from O, (2) the projection of 3D velocity P-dot to 2D velocity p-dot where the end points are collinear with O via a secondary projection ray, and (3) the 1/Z depth-scaling effect of optical flow where increasing Z reduces the image flow magnitude. It also shows radial expansion when motion is directed toward the camera (Z-dot < 0).
evaluation.notes: The figure is exceptionally well-implemented, achieving perfect scores in both concept accuracy and interactivity. It clearly demonstrates perspective projection, 3D to 2D velocity mapping, and the 1/Z depth-scaling of optical flow using an interactive depth slider, motion direction toggle, and clickable 3D mesh elements. No critical errors or conceptual misunderstandings were identified.
